data.title: I want to pay off $4,500 in credit-card debt in 2 months. Is this possible?
data.description:
By Aditi Shrikant

'I'm 32 years old and feel like I should know how to do this stuff by now'

"Every time I get close to paying it off, I need to use my card for some medical bill or emergency expenses."

Dear Dollar Signs,

I cannot seem to get out of credit-card debt no matter what I do. It's not a lot - about $4,500 - but it's weighing on me. Every time I get close to paying it off, I need to use my card for some medical bill or emergency expenses. It feels like I'm never out of the hole. I'm 32 years old and feel like I should know how to do this stuff by now.

I have about $1,000 in savings, but I don't want to put that toward these emergencies because then I feel like I'll have nothing.

I'd love to pay this off by the end of the year. Do you have any tips?

Fiscally Flustered

If you're just starting out on your money or career journey and have questions about how to navigate your finances, we want to hear from you. Write to Dollar Signs, MarketWatch's new advice column, at dollarsigns@marketwatch.com.

Dear Flustered,

I feel for you. A relatively low amount of credit-card debt can be easy to neglect - and I've definitely done it myself. But putting it off and carrying a balance will, as I'm sure you know, negatively affect your credit score. And the interest on your balance ensures that even if you stop making purchases, your debt will grow. It doesn't help that credit-card APRs have been going up in recent years, making credit-card debt more expensive.

I'll be honest: I don't think you'll be able to pay this off by the end of the year. There are 10 weeks left in 2026, meaning you'd have to direct $450 a week (not including interest) to this debt. That is a lot of money, and I assume if you were earning enough to do this, you would have by now. This will take a bit longer.

You need a six- to 12-month "financial reset," according to Mark La Spisa, a certified financial planner based in Barrington, Ill.

You are right not to touch that $1,000. Keep it as an emergency reserve and work on allocating some of your monthly cash flow toward your debt. After you pay for your housing, groceries and utilities, how much money is left and what is it going toward? Most people are not spending all their disposable income wisely. The best way to find out where exactly you can cut spending is to look at your bank statements for the last 90 days.

"I'd specifically look for $300- to $500-per-month expenses that can temporarily be redirected toward the cards," La Spisa said.

Perhaps you order a lot of takeout food or call ride-hailing services frequently. Redirect those funds to your credit-card bill. I often find that I'm subscribed to far more streaming services than I actually use.

Once you decide the amount of money you want to put toward this bill each month, automate payments on payday. Don't even let the money hit your checking account.

Any random windfalls, such as a tax refund or work bonus, should also go toward paying off your credit-card bill.

"Look for one-time accelerators," La Spisa said. "A $4,000 problem can often be solved surprisingly quickly."

I know this can be hard. I often justify impulse purchases by telling myself that my money is supposed to bring me some happiness. While this is true, I can never truly enjoy a nice meal out or a new pair of shoes if any amount of debt is hanging over my head.

"We're not asking you to live this way forever," La Spisa said. "We're going to live differently for several months so you can stop carrying this debt forever."

How to become more financially aware

I do find it concerning that you don't know where to start when it comes to paying down this debt. To me, this signals that you aren't very aware of where your money is going.

Your first priority should be to pay off this $4,500, but the work doesn't stop there. You want to build and practice healthy spending habits, so that you don't end up in this position again and you can continue to build up your emergency savings fund. Experts recommend you have six months to a year worth of expenses saved.

"The real victory isn't paying off the $4,000," La Spisa said. "It's turning the $400 to $600 a month they were sending to credit-card companies into a permanent savings habit. That can materially change their long-term financial trajectory."

Research suggests that having $2,000 in cash saved for emergencies can meaningfully improve your sense of financial stability.

The exercise of reviewing your bank statements isn't a one-time thing. Regularly re-evaluate where your money is going, and what you need and enjoy.

You are young, and this isn't a crushing amount of debt. If you create a realistic budget and learn to live within it, you'll be able to pay off your debt and become a more savvy spender and saver.

Write to Dollar Signs at dollarsigns@marketwatch.com.

By submitting your story to Dow Jones & Co., the publisher of MarketWatch, you understand and agree that we may use your story, or versions of it, in all media and platforms.

-Aditi Shrikant

DIRECTV Adds NHL's New Carolina Hurricanes, Columbus Blue Jackets, Minnesota Wild, and St. Louis Blues Regional Channels

DIRECTV Adds NHL's New Carolina Hurricanes, Columbus Blue Jackets, Minnesota Wild, and St. Louis Blues Regional Channels

PR Newswire

EL SEGUNDO, Calif., Oct. 24, 2026

EL SEGUNDO, Calif., Oct. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- DIRECTV today announced a new multi-year distribution agreement with the National Hockey League for Hurricanes Hockey Network, Blue Jackets Hockey Network, Wild+, and Blue Note+ pregame, postgame, and in-game live sports services.

Each of the four channels will be available to DIRECTV streaming and satellite customers who live in each team's NHL-designated home territory and subscribe to Choice and higher packages, and each U-verse customer in those same regions who subscribes to U200 and above.

This agreement also provides distribution rights to each NHL team to all of DIRECTV FOR BUSINESS's thousands of sports bars, restaurants, fitness clubs, and other commercial venues located within each team's respective region.

DIRECTV has recently obtained regional or local rights to provide 76 of the 81 U.S.-based NHL, NBA, or MLB franchises to their local fans, including multi-year agreements for 23 U.S.-based hockey teams.

"We are committed to keeping fans connected to their favorite teams and giving them more choice and flexibility in how they watch and what they pay," said Rob Thun, Chief Content Officer at DIRECTV. "As local sports distribution evolves, DIRECTV brings team channels, regional sports networks, and other viewing options together to make it easier for fans to follow the teams they love. We're pleased to work with the NHL, NBA, MLB, and others to deliver that experience."

"We're thrilled that fans of the Carolina Hurricanes, Columbus Blue Jackets, Minnesota Wild, and St. Louis Blues can now watch their favorite team on DIRECTV in their local market, said David Proper, NHL Chief Media Officer and Senior Executive Vice President. "Making it easy for fans to follow their teams is at the heart of what we do. This agreement puts our clubs in four passionate hockey markets in front of more of their fans, and that's a win for everyone who loves the game."

  • Carolina Hurricanes local games are available on channel 650 (streaming, satellite) and 1726/726 (U-verse).
  • Columbus Blue Jackets local games are available on channel 660 (streaming), 660-1 (satellite) and 1735/735 (U-verse).
  • Minnesota Wild local games are available on channel 668 (streaming), 668-1 (satellite) and 1745/745 (U-verse).
  • St. Louis Blues local games are available on channel 673 (streaming and satellite) and 1747/747 (U-verse).

As the local sports landscape continues to transition and teams move to different forms of local distribution, it has become more complex for providers like DIRECTV to ensure that all the fans who previously enjoyed games can still receive them. data.title: Over 40% of Americans are heading toward retirement 'blind' - with no plan
data.description:
By Jessica Hall

Nearly half of Americans haven't calculated what they'll need in retirement

Start running the numbers on your retirement plan as early as possible, advisers say.

Americans may be walking into retirement blindfolded.

A total of 42% of Americans have never calculated how much money they'll need in retirement, according to a new report from Evergreen.ai, a financial-planning platform. Even those closer to retirement are dodging the task: One-third of those who expected to retire within the next 15 years have avoided running their retirement numbers, per the report.

"People are busy, and people don't want bad news. They don't want to know if they have a shortfall, they don't want to hear they shouldn't buy that new car or whatnot. It's human nature," said Joseph Spada, a private wealth adviser with Summit Financial in Parsippany, N.J.

Yet at a time when 67% of Americans fear running out of money more than death, according to the Allianz Center for the Future of Retirement, it's important to know your retirement number as early as possible. Many Americans are ill-prepared for retirement, with the median amount that workers have saved for retirement at just $955, according to the National Institute of Retirement Security. That's a small fraction of the $1.2 million that Americans think they'll need to retire comfortably, according to Schroders, an asset-management firm.

"It's the most common fear there is: running out of money. But unless you have a plan, there's a risk you won't have enough," said Christopher Walsh, a senior financial adviser and regional marketing director at Capital Choice Arizona in Phoenix. "Coming up with a plan is mitigating the fear of not knowing. The longer you go without a plan, the bigger the risk is of running out of money or not having enough.

"The more time you give yourself, the more flexibility you have to fix things," Walsh added. "Sitting on the sidelines gives you fewer choices, and often suboptimal choices."

Without knowledge of your retirement number, you could be forced to work longer than you want to, and retiring may be a luxury you can't afford. But needing to work until you die may be risky. Not everyone can choose when they retire, as some are forced to do so sooner than they anticipated because of bad health, caregiving responsibilities or job cuts.

Most retirees - 3 in 5 - reported retiring earlier than age 65, with a median retirement age of 62, according to the Employee Benefit Research Institute. Nearly half of retirees said they retired earlier than planned, EBRI found.

Not knowing your retirement number also puts you at risk of severe lifestyle shock. If you retire without actually having enough money in retirement, you may have to severely cut back on your spending in retirement, especially as people are living longer and retirement can now last decades. Distributing too much money too soon can make the fears of running out of money a reality.

"Finding out at 45 that you're behind gives you time to adjust your savings, investments or retirement expectations. Finding out at 65 leaves you with far fewer options," said Jon Ulin, founder and managing principal at Ulin & Co. Wealth Management in Boca Raton, Fla. "Not knowing your lump-sum retirement-savings number is like driving blind into one of the biggest financial decisions of your life. ... You can't simply wake up in your 50s or 60s, decide you're done working and expect the numbers to work."

Where to begin

Start by listing all of your expenditures and income.

"Find out really what you're spending - it's always more than you think," Spada said. "Find out your essential spending versus your discretionary spending. See what you can cut out and what has to be there."

Some expenses may disappear in retirement, such as a mortgage payment once you pay off your house, or college tuition and other costs associated with raising children. Others expenses may increase, such as the cost of healthcare. A 65-year-old retiring in 2026 can expect to spend an average of $185,500 on healthcare and medical expenses throughout retirement, according to Fidelity Investments. That estimate doesn't include long-term care.

While working with a financial adviser may give you a more nuanced picture of what you need in retirement, there are several retirement calculators online that may do the job sufficiently - so long as the person using the calculator is providing accurate data. There are also some retirement rules of thumb: One estimates needing 80% of your annual income in retirement; another is the 4% rule, which suggests withdrawing that much in the first year of retirement and then adjusting for inflation. These are just suggestions, however; some people spend more while others spend less, and these guidelines are bound to change.

Areas that people often overlook include inflation, healthcare expenses, taxes and market downturns, said Aaron Gaines, founder and president of Gaines Capital Management in Smyrna, Ga.

Next steps

One you've estimated your annual retirement expenses, subtract guaranteed income like Social Security benefits and pensions, and multiply the remaining gap by 25, Gaines said. For example, if you need $40,000 annually from your investments, that suggests a starting target of $1 million.

"One of the biggest mistakes Americans make is approaching retirement without knowing what retirement will actually cost. Your retirement number isn't just about how much you've saved. It's about how much income your savings need to produce for the rest of your life," Gaines said. "The goal isn't necessarily to retire with the most money. It's to retire knowing you won't outlive it."

Even Social Security may not be guaranteed. Social Security benefits may be cut by 26% in 2032 unless Congress acts to shore up the system, according to the Congressional Budget Office. There are proposals that would reform the program and thus potentially alter benefits, such as raising the full retirement age.

Be conservative in your planning, said Robert Persichitte, a financial planner and founder of Delagify Financial in Arvada, Colo. "Regardless of your financial plan or tax planning, living within your means is the most critical skill to retire safely - don't get overconfident," he said.

The important step is just to start - as early as possible.

"If you run your model now and it's bad news, you want to know about it now. There's not much you can do to fix things at 60," Spada said. "Create your own retirement model now, even if you're 15 years out. A lot can go wrong in those 15 years, but it's a starting point."

-Jessica Hall

data.title: Axon Announces Body 5: Next-Generation Camera Built for the AI Era
data.description:
Axon Announces Body 5: Next-Generation Camera Built for the AI Era

Axon Announces Body 5: Next-Generation Camera Built for the AI Era

PR Newswire

SCOTTSDALE, Ariz., Oct. 24, 2026

Axon Body 5 delivers 25x the AI processing power of earlier-generation cameras, with upgraded connectivity, audio and battery life to support real-time situational awareness in the field

SCOTTSDALE, Ariz., Oct. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Axon (Nasdaq: AXON), the global leader in public safety technology, today announced Axon Body 5, its newest body-worn camera designed to bring more powerful intelligence, connectivity and real-time support directly to officers in the field.

For years, Axon body cameras have helped agencies capture critical evidence and create greater transparency. Body 5 is built to help officers during the call, with information, assistance and backup on the spot.

"Officers shouldn't have to choose between getting information and watching the scene. With Axon Body 5, they don't," said Rick Smith, Axon Founder and CEO. "They capture a license or document with the camera, keep their hands free and eyes up, and get information faster than writing it down and calling it in by radio. An officer fully engaged with the person in front of them, not down at a notepad, is a safer officer and a better-served community."

Axon Body 5: Built for the AI Era

Built from the ground up for the AI era, Axon Body 5 delivers 25x the AI processing power than earlier generation Axon body cameras, alongside advancements in connectivity, audio, video and battery life. Together, these upgrades give the camera the physical power to run smarter AI features — both today and as new AI tools are developed in the future — while also making it more dependable for officers to use every day. 

For the first time, Axon is also introducing two versions of its latest flagship camera: Axon Body 5 and Axon Body 5 Pro.

Both models feature several key advancements, including:

  • 25x more processing power for AI: A powerful new computing architecture creates the capacity to support current and future AI features directly on the body camera.
  • Enhanced video: Improved video captures clearer evidence across challenging environments, including better low-light performance.
  • Improved connectivity: Seamless connectivity in urban and remote environments - and more precise location capability - helps officers, cameras and remote support teams stay connected when timely information matters most.
  • Longer battery life: 20% more battery life than the previous generation helps keep the camera ready and connected throughout an officer's shift.

The Axon Body 5 Pro will continue to gain new AI capabilities as they become available, growing along with the AI Era Plan. Additionally, new hardware features include:

  • A near-focus camera: An additional dedicated camera lens lets officers scan driver's licenses to check status and search for wants or warrants in seconds, without returning to the patrol vehicle, with relevant information sent to Axon Fusus to support real-time operations.
  • Front-facing speakers: Four additional speakers project even more powerful audio toward the person an officer is speaking with, helping real-time translations from Axon Assistant carry more clearly over heavy traffic or crowd noise. 
  • Additional memory: Extra space lets the camera run several AI tools at once, helping officers stay better informed and work faster.

Bringing More of Axon's AI Era Into the Field

Axon Body 5 helps officers get more out of the Axon AI Era Plan by bringing smart tools right to the scene. Axon's portfolio already supports public safety professionals across a growing range of tasks. For example, Draft One helps officers turn body-camera audio into high-quality report drafts and Axon Assistant provides voice-based information access and real-time translation.

Increasingly, Axon is also bringing AI into real-time operations.

Axon Guardian is a new category of AI features within the AI Era Plan that was specifically created to work with an officer's field-based devices - starting with body cameras and in-car cameras - to improve safety. Guardian is designed to flag potential risks as situations unfold and create alerts when additional attention may be needed. Two of the first features include:

  • Escalation Detection: When an Axon Body 4 or Axon Body 5 camera is activated and recording, Guardian has the ability to detect potential conflicts in real time and create an alert in Axon Fusus. A human reviews the livestream and decides if additional support or action is needed.
  • Approach Alert: When active on Axon Fleet 3, Guardian can detect if the door of a stopped vehicle opens and alert the officer through the in-car display and their body-worn camera.

Combined, Axon Body 5 and the expanding AI Era portfolio demonstrate the importance of AI as a critical resource to assist public safety professionals before, during and after an incident — reducing administrative burden, improving situational awareness and helping protect more lives.

Innovating Responsibly

Axon's Responsible Innovation framework guides the development of all of its products. Designed with this in mind, Axon Body 5 and Guardian prioritize human oversight and maintain agency control over data. As a key part of the responsible innovation process, Axon's independent Ethics and Equity Advisory Council was created to help responsibly develop and deploy new technologies with transparency, while aligning with community expectations.

General availability dates for Axon Body 5 and Axon Guardian will be announced soon. Product features and capabilities vary by configuration. For more information on Axon's current products and services: Axon Product Catalog - Axon.com.

About Axon
Axon (Nasdaq: AXON) is the global leader in public safety technology supporting state, local, federal and international public safety agencies with technology designed to Protect Life. Complementing its mission, Axon's growing Enterprise market focuses on protecting critical infrastructure and frontline workers across multiple industries including corporate security, hospitality, retail and healthcare. Founder-led since 1993, Axon builds products with transparency and responsibility. From TASER energy devices to today's connected network of hardware - including cameras, drones, and robotics - cloud software, sensors, and AI-tools, the Axon ecosystem helps seamlessly protect people and places when it matters most. To ensure these technologies align with community expectations, Axon's independent Ethics & Equity Advisory Council guides the ethical, inclusive, and accountable design of its products and services. Learn more about the EEAC and Axon's Responsible Innovation framework at Axon Responsibility. 

Non-Axon trademarks are the property of their respective owners. Axon, TASER and the Delta Logo are trademarks of Axon Enterprise, Inc., some of which are registered in the US and other countries. For more information, visit www.axon.com/legal. All rights reserved.

Please visit https://investor.axon.com and https://www.axon.com/newsroom for more information.

Kate MacKinnon
Vice President, Communications
press@axon.com

data.title: Elon Musk promised a SpaceX share to every kid in America - don't hold your breath
data.description:
By Brett Arends

Trick or treat? Musk has a long record of saying things that have little relation to reality.

Elon Musk wants to give American kids shares in SpaceX. Maybe.

Elon Musk says he will give away one share of his future-intergalactic-empire company SpaceX "to every kid in America" next year.

But America's 72 million children, as well as their parents, should probably hold off on the celebrations for now.

Musk is an extraordinary, even brilliant, man in many ways, but he has a long and abysmal record of saying things - especially on Twitter, or X - that turn out to have little relation to reality. Or none at all.

Like the time he randomly and falsely accused a complete stranger on the other side of the world of being a child molester, simply because the man had disagreed with him? (Musk even doubled down on the accusation, before eventually admitting it was all made-up.)

Or the time he announced he had the financing to take Tesla private, causing enormous turmoil in the markets? Yeah, no - he didn't. Musk and Tesla had to pay $20 million each to settle with the SEC over the affair.

And the time he said he was willing to buy Twitter, only to try to back out of the deal? (He agreed to follow through on the offer once Twitter sued him.)

Only last year he said he had discovered millions of dead people claiming Social Security.

Once again: Yeah, no.

Two years ago, in an attempt to influence the 2024 presidential election, he promised to shower millions of dollars on people who registered to vote and signed a petition.

Musk has only just settled the lawsuits from all the angry people who say they were misled. Terms of the settlement weren't disclosed. But Musk made sure to settle before he had to testify under oath - always a good sign.

It's also two years since he promised U.S. taxpayers that he would find "$2 trillion" in savings in the federal budget by uncovering waste, fraud and abuse. All we had to do was give him the U.S. president he wanted.

Well, he got his wish, but we never saw the savings. Musk slashed the promise in half before Donald Trump even took office. In the end, federal spending went up this year by 5.5% to $7.4 trillion. That's $600 billion more than it was during Joe Biden's last year in the White House.

And Musk's pal Trump has just proposed the first $8 trillion federal budget in history.

But, hey, Musk got a free chainsaw out of it.

There was no accountability, no apology, no mea culpa. Musk went on Joe Rogan and blamed his failure on a vast, shadowy and mysterious conspiracy against him.

The truth is out there.

All of this is to say that you shouldn't be surprised if these SpaceX shares (SPCX) never end up in your children's accounts. Maybe they will. Maybe they won't. Trick or treat!

The second thing is that your children will need to get a so-called Trump account to get the shares. Musk says he will donate the stock through those accounts. Trump accounts, or 530A accounts, are brilliant tax dodges set up by the president and his sidekicks on Capitol Hill that mostly benefit trust-fund kids. They are a poor deal, or no deal at all, for most other children. Their main value is the $1,000 in "free" money, transferred from U.S. taxpayers, given to children born during Donald Trump's presidential term. (Really.)

The third thing to bear in mind about Musk's proposed giveaway is that, while one share of SpaceX is better than no shares, the value is currently $150. And if your kids try to cash it in, they will owe capital-gains tax.

So this gift isn't going to make a material difference to your child's life. I'm not being churlish. Free money is free money. I'm just saying this isn't Oprah giving you a new car. Musk is giving you a child's bicycle from Walmart.

And it's not merely altruistic. We can never read another person's mind, and Elon Musk didn't respond to my email requests, so I can't tell you for certain what he's thinking.

But it is surely not a coincidence that he is making this offer so publicly two weeks before an election that he is desperately trying to influence. Musk has already spent $280 million to help save his favored Republicans from voters. (It also came on the heels of the AI company Anthropic's announcement it would commit a portion of its shares to a "public benefit fund," with possibly more to come as the company grows.)

And this is business. SpaceX depends on the U.S. government for about 20% of its revenue. This company, like his other publicly traded operation, Tesla (TSLA), is heavily exposed to federal spending, regulations and laws. Musk wants as many friends in Washington as he can get.

His grandiose offer is excellent marketing for SpaceX. There is very good research that finds, as you would expect, consumers tend to like a company more if they own stock in it.

Musk is effectively hoping to buy 72 million young SpaceX fans. Maybe they will be motivated to use the SpaceX AI bot, called Grok, instead of its many competitors, like Gemini, Claude, Perplexity or Chat GPT. Maybe they will be more friendly toward Musk in future years when he tries to extract more money from the taxpayers. Who knows? It can't hurt.

And the cost to him really isn't onerous. While Musk is saying he will give away 72 million shares, that's barely 1% of his stock. In total, including options and restricted stock, his ownership in SpaceX totals 6.4 billion shares, valued currently at $960 billion.

Musk won't have to pay a penny. He will simply transfer paper. He could not cash out all of those 6.4 billion shares anyway, so his actual sacrifice is nonexistent.

But first things first. Believe the giveaway only when you see it.

-Brett Arends

data.title: The Social Security Administration wants more babies signed up for 'Trump accounts.' But there's still a catch.
data.description:
By Jessica Hall

Social Security is looking to reverse an initially slow uptake on Trump accounts

President Donald Trump gives a pen to a child during an event about "Trump accounts" in the Oval Office on Oct. 7.

The Social Security Administration just made it a little easier for parents to sign up their newborns for "Trump accounts" - investment accounts for children under 18 - but the move falls short of a hoped-for auto-enrollment process.

The SSA will now include information about Trump accounts with Social Security cards issued to newborns through the so-called "enumeration at birth" program. The insert provides instructions for claiming an eligible child's account through the Trump Accounts app. Babies born between 2025 and 2028 are eligible to receive $1,000 in seed money for these accounts from the U.S. Department of Treasury.

This extra push by the Social Security Administration follows an announcement by President Donald Trump earlier this month that each child would be automatically enrolled, after slow initial uptake on the accounts.

"Anything you can do to simplify the process helps. But we're still far from fully automatic," said Ray Boshara, a senior policy adviser at Washington University in St. Louis and the Aspen Institute Financial Security Program, who has helped policymakers develop plans for children's savings accounts.

Information from this insert from the Social Security Administration will accompany Social Security cards for newborns.

The tax-advantaged investment accounts, which are officially known as 530A accounts, were initially promoted as a way to help children build wealth starting from an early age. Research has found that small, consistent contributions to investment accounts over a lifetime are a reliable way to accumulate wealth, even for low earners. The accounts have contribution limits and at the outset were to be invested in index funds.

The insert details how parents can access their newborn's Trump account.

Philanthropists, employers and businesses offered additional seed money for these accounts, including Michael and Susan Dell, who pledged $6.25 billion in cash to the accounts of children meeting age and geographic benchmarks.

Earlier this year, SpaceX (SPCX) President Gwynne Shotwell promised to donate about 2 million shares of the company's stock. Elon Musk on Monday said he would give "every kid in America" a share of SpaceX next year.

Along with Social Security cards mailed to newborns, the Social Security Administration will include an information sheet that directs parents to visit TrumpAccounts.gov to download the Trump Accounts app and sign up. It also will alert them to look for a communication from the Treasury Department with information about activating the account and receiving the $1,000 contribution, if the child is eligible.

"Every time you're asking parents, especially low-income parents, to get through more hoops, they won't get there. They still need to activate the account and it's a separate process to claim the $1,000," Boshara said.

Only 5% of low- and moderate-income families have opened a Trump account for their children, according to a survey published in September by Commonwealth, a nonprofit organization. The top barriers to participating were concerns about the impact on taxes or public benefits, the inability to afford monetary contributions for their accounts and lack of trust in the Trump administration, Commonwealth said.

On Oct. 1, the Trump administration created Trump accounts for more than 60 million children. That was a big step toward smoothing the enrollment process, but the accounts still need to be claimed by parents to manage them and to allow family members, friends and employers to contribute.

The latest move to have the Social Security Administration provide the information for newborns' parents also may help, but it may not go far enough to allay concerns and increase signups, said Juan Hernandez-Ariano, founder and principal of WealthCreate in Houston.

"I think it helps that it starts with Social Security, but the emails don't come from Social Security. They come from 'no-reply@TrumpAccounts.Treasury.gov.' It's a legitimate domain and there's nothing that screams red flag, but we've been taught as consumers that Treasury and Social Security don't really send emails, they send letters in the mail, so I feel like it adds another layer of resistance for some clients," Hernandez-Ariano said.

"There are just a lot of novelties here for people, and I can see that not 100% of people would participate, even the ones who raised their hand originally, because it looks different than what you'd expect, so I don't think easier instructions by themselves will move signups that much," Hernandez-Ariano said.

About 3.6 million babies are born in the U.S. each year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's National Center for Health Statistics.

"Families do need to take additional steps to access the funds for which their children are eligible. So far as that goes, it's a good thing for SSA to inform families how to access a benefit that will help their children. I think it's safe to assume more families will activate their accounts because of SSA's outreach," said Kathleen Romig, director of Social Security and disability policy at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a progressive think tank.

Romig, however, said that the SSA's message to the public was concerning.

"The agency has a responsibility to provide nonpartisan information to the public. However, the press release frames it as a '$1,000 gift to a Trump account from the U.S. Treasury Department.' This money is not a gift from President Trump nor from his administration, though the naming and framing of the accounts may lead people to believe that it is. In fact, the accounts are a government program passed by Congress and funded through taxpayer dollars," Romig said. "SSA's wide distribution of this message, to an audience well beyond the new parents whose children are eligible for the $1,000, is particularly concerning two weeks before a consequential election."

-Jessica Hall

data.title: Walmart, Best Buy and other stores now use digital price tags. Critics say they could lead to different prices for different shoppers.
data.description:
By Genna Contino

Retailers say digital shelf labels save labor and cut checkout errors, but consumer advocates warn they pave the way for dynamic pricing in brick-and-mortar stores

Digital shelf labels have been replacing paper price tags at major retailers.

Store aisles are getting a digital makeover.

Major retailers such as Best Buy (BBY), Kroger (KR) and Walmart (WMT) have begun replacing paper price tags with electronic shelf labels: a small digital screen displaying the item's price. Walmart started rolling out the digital labels in 2024, and announced plans this year to install them across its more than 4,600 U.S. stores by the end of the year.

While retailers say the transition will create more accurate pricing, deliver instant discounts for shoppers and free up time for employees, consumer advocates worry the digital labels are a way to bring dynamic pricing to brick-and-mortar stores. Dynamic or algorithmic pricing is when a business changes prices in real time based on market conditions such as demand, inventory and competitor rates. This practice is standard in the airline and ride-hailing industries, and a growing number of retailers have started using it in recent years.

"This idea that we could be eliminating the price tag altogether in part because price variation is going to be so institutionalized is really worrying," said Lindsay Owens, executive director of Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive think tank that has criticized companies' use of dynamic pricing. The traditional price tag "offers stability, which is so important for budgeting. It offers transparency, which is so important for comparison shopping, which isn't just important for the budget shopper, it's how the entire economy is kept competitive."

Retail trade groups, however, reject the claim that digital tags are designed to manipulate prices to rip off consumers. Jason Straczewski, group vice president of government relations and political affairs at the National Retail Federation, said state and federal law requires the price advertised on the shelf label to match the price at the point of sale, and that digital shelf labels can actually improve price accuracy between the shelf and the register.

Critics, including Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, have suggested stores could use facial recognition along with digital price tags to show different prices to different consumers. That's not the case, Straczewski said. "These price tags are literally powered by a watch battery," Straczewski said. "They're not hardwired into some system that's connected to the internet to an algorithmic computer center somewhere in the back of the house."

Walmart, for example, said all customers will see the same price on the labels, which "modernize how prices are displayed, not how they're decided" - but the labels do have a light-up feature to help employees and shoppers who are using the store's app find items. "It knows that you're in that particular store and you can be in 'store mode,'" said Walmart spokesperson Robyn Babbitt. "If you're searching for something, it will allow you to light up the [label]."

A Walmart associate uses the light-up feature on a digital shelf label to find an item.

In a response to criticism from Owens specifically, the big-box store said it "does not and will not use digital shelf labels for individual or dynamic pricing." Best Buy and Kroger did not respond to requests for comment.

Despite industry assurances, lawmakers and regulators are monitoring the expanding technology. New Jersey implemented a one-year moratorium on electronic shelf labels this summer "while the New Jersey Innovation Authority studies the effects and impact of that technology." Maryland passed legislation this year requiring prices on electronic shelf labels at grocery stores to remain fixed for at least one business day and prohibiting stores from using customer data to set individualized prices. A proposed state Senate bill would prohibit them in supermarkets and pharmacies in New York, where a poll found that 64% of New Yorkers think the labels would push up the cost of groceries.

The Federal Trade Commission also proposed a policy statement in August targeting personalized pricing, warning that retailers using personal data to set custom prices without clear disclosures violate federal law.

For years Americans have had "a reasonable expectation that if you and I were shopping for the same item at the same time, we'd pay the same price," Owens said. "And that, I think, is really eroding."

-Genna Contino

data.title: My partner of 17 years left me his $1 million home. His children are crying foul. Am I obliged to split it with them?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'I never paid rent, although I put $45,000 toward a new kitchen and a roof'

"I liked them, and they were always respectful of my role in their father's life." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

My late partner, "Daniel," kept the radio on a classical music station all day, and he was a keen gardener. He was a romantic at heart, and yet he never once asked me to marry him. We didn't need to. I never thought it was a requirement to get married to satisfy other people's social conventions, especially later in life. I was 51 and he was 59 when we met, both of us divorced and both (somewhat) wary. Marriage didn't come up, and that suited us. We kept separate bank accounts and I moved into the house he'd bought in 1998. I stayed for 17 years.

Daniel died six months ago, at 76. The house is now worth roughly $1 million or more, and it has no mortgage. I never paid rent, although I put $45,000 toward a new kitchen and a roof. We both always called it his house, but it was still our home for the best part of two decades.

His three children are 44, 41 and 38, and they live in three different states. They came to see us four or five times a year. I'm told the oldest son rang every Sunday. The youngest son brought the grandchildren and they came with a lot of noise, which Daniel loved. The third child, his daughter, kept in touch regularly. They all got along, more or less. I wasn't super close to his kids but I liked them, and they were always respectful of my role in their father's life.

'He did have very mild cognitive impairment, but no dementia diagnosis.'

About three years ago, he changed his will. The house goes to me, while the $600,000 in retirement accounts and cash goes to his children. Daniel had watched friends' widows get pushed into selling their homes because the kids wanted their share, and he didn't want that for me. I had about $250,000 of my own in cash and stocks, in addition to my Social Security and a small private pension, and I could rent, but I couldn't buy a $1 million house.

I drove him to appointments. After his stroke two years before he died, I helped him dress on difficult mornings. He recovered well, but he stopped driving and lost his footing.

One of his children now says a conversation about his estate planning proves I planted the idea. He did have very mild cognitive impairment, but no dementia diagnosis. He'd forget names and repeat himself, but he was otherwise fine. Daniel still managed his own investments and made his own medical decisions. His lawyer met with him alone, and his doctor later told me he understood his finances.

His daughter pointed out that I drove him to the lawyer's office. I made the appointment because he asked me to. She says I should have insisted one of the children come. I thought that would have insulted a grown man. I don't think any of them are bad people. They're grieving. They lost their father and the house they grew up visiting at the same time. They've asked me to sell and split the proceeds four ways. They call it fair.

But I was his family, too. I don't want to fight them or spend years in court, and I also don't want to hand back something Daniel chose to give me. Should I sell the house and split it four ways?

The Widow

Related: After 46 years working, I'm not retiring - instead, I take a vacation every month. Is that a good life in your 70s?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

It's possible to have some cognitive impairment or even dementia and still have testamentary capacity.

Dear Widow,

First, you aren't wrong to abide by his wishes for a home and security for you.

All bets were off when your late partner died. When your partner - I keep typing "your husband" because that's what he feels like from your letter - left this world, so, it seems, did your social connection to his three children, and they have decided that there's not much left between you to sustain. Any pretense at acceptance has long been discarded. However, they do believe that you are standing in the way of them and their inheritance, this $1.1 million house. To be fair to the children, they are grieving and may be angry and confused.

Sometimes it's the central relationship in a family that holds everyone together. People often make assumptions about inheritances before the time comes, so we can understand how Daniel's children might have allowed their expectations to get ahead of reality. They may start pulling soft strings - saying he felt guilted into making this decision or that he was not of sound mind when he made it - to see if you acquiesce. If expensive, public and emotionally draining lawsuits can be avoided, they should be, and these grown children appear to be avoiding that course of action, for now.

It's possible to have cognitive impairment or even dementia and still have testamentary capacity. Daniel's doctor and lawyer could testify to that in court. A dementia diagnosis does not mean a person lacks testamentary capacity to change a will. The legal basis for this goes back to a landmark English case, Banks v. Goodfellow, from 1870. The court in that case found that John Banks, a wealthy man, was of sound mind, despite mental-health challenges, when he made a will. In the U.S., each state sets its own standard, although many are similar.

There are two issues at hand: capacity and undue influence. It would not hurt to get legal advice now and get your ducks in a row, just in case Daniel's three children take this further. But the burden of proof would rest on their shoulders. After 17 years with Daniel, I would - from a nonlegal, hunch perspective - think you had a pretty good case. It was not like you were Daniel's caregiver or someone from his nursing home who, over a period of months, decided to "fall in love" and convince him to change his will.

Don't miss: I'm a 68-year-old widow and give money to my two adult children. Am I putting my retirement at risk?

Marriage affords protection

Daniel's legal capacity can be supported with evidence, and the more you have, the better. That includes signed statements from attorneys, doctors and witnesses that your late partner understood the new will when he signed it. Find an estate-planning or elder-law attorney to help you navigate the process, should it come to that. Other medical records, even a video of the signing, can help illustrate the absence of any coercion or undue influence. Since the will was signed about three years ago, ask the lawyer for his file notes and the doctor for Daniel's medical records.

Marriage would have afforded you more protection and perhaps made it easier for you to stand your ground now. When a second spouse inherits everything, they can write a will and leave the entire estate to their own children, a subsequent spouse or even their favorite charities, cutting off the deceased spouse's biological children. A life estate, depending on how it was set up, could have given you the right to live in the home for the remainder of your days. But because you weren't married, the will is your main legal protection.

Some states have "homestead" laws that apply to married and unmarried couples, and a small number of states allow couples to enter into common-law marriage. Case in point: Texas is a community-property state, so anything you purchased prior to a marriage is separate property. A surviving spouse has the right to occupy the homestead for the rest of their lives, even if it is separate property or was gifted to a third party. Marital trusts are popular for blended families as a way to pass assets to a surviving spouse and still protect children's inheritance.

Your response to his three children's accusations is a compassionate one. They are grieving. On the one hand, they are weaponizing your acts of kindness, like driving Daniel to medical appointments, as acts of control and perhaps attempts to infantilize him. On the other hand, they are twisting the facts - such as you not being able to afford to buy a house anywhere near the size of your current home - and turning that, too, into some kind of manipulation on your part. Find out about the statute of limitations for contesting a will and whether this one had a no-contest clause.

After that, go about your life and be good to yourself. You are grieving, too.

Related: 'We lived within our means': I earned $30,000 as a pastor and still retired comfortably. Why don't you tell people that?

By emailing your questions to The Moneyist or posting your dilemmas on The Moneyist Facebook group, you agree to have them published anonymously on MarketWatch.

'I'm never selling': I'm 47 and buy bitcoin with every dollar I earn. Am I crazy?

I'm 77, pay rent and live off Social Security, but I help homeless people. Why are so many people going hungry?

Check out The Moneyist's private Facebook group, where members help answer life's thorniest money issues. Post your questions, or weigh in on the latest Moneyist columns.

By submitting your story to Dow Jones & Co., the publisher of MarketWatch, you understand and agree that we may use your story, or versions of it, in all media and platforms, including via third parties.

-Quentin Fottrell

data.title: Retire on 8% a year with little or no risk? How to use annuities the right way.
data.description:
By Brett Arends

But always check the fine print

Higher guaranteed income: What's not to like?

Market turmoil has created a remarkable opportunity in recent weeks for retirees and those seeking secure, stable income for life.

Annuities can provide retirees with a guaranteed income for the rest of their life. Immediate or income annuities, which are insurance contracts that convert a lump sum into a stream of income, have just seen payout rates rocket to their highest levels since around the time of the global financial crisis nearly 20 years ago.

Those annual payout rates have risen as much as half a percentage point in just a few weeks, following the late summer selloff in the bond market. Insurance companies that sell these annuities use Treasury and investment-grade corporate bonds to finance them. As bond markets fell and long-term interest rates rose, insurance companies raised payout rates.

As a result of the market moves, a 65-year-old man can earn a guaranteed income for life of 8.4% on an investment, and a 65-year-old woman could see 8%. In other words, if you invested $100,000 in an immediate or income annuity right now, as a man you'd earn $8,400 a year and as a woman you'd earn $8,000 until you died.

If you are worried about inflation - and who isn't right now? - you can buy an annuity that raises those payouts by, say, 3% every year. In exchange, your starting payout rates at 65 would be lower: 6.4% if you're a man or 6.1% if you're a woman.

(The payout rates for women are lower because they live longer, on average. Actuarially, they work out to be the same.)

Guaranteed income

I'm certainly not running an advertorial for insurance companies and annuities, but there is no doubt that mathematically, they provide the highest possible guaranteed lifetime income out of a lump sum. That's because they work as a form of life insurance, and those people who buy an annuity and die young effectively subsidize those who live to be very old.

Financial planners often talk about a 4% or 4.5% rule, which means that when you retire, you can withdraw 4% of your assets in your first year, raise those withdrawal amounts each year in line with inflation, and have an excellent chance of making your money last until you die.

Those who buy an annuity give up liquidity: The money is tied up, effectively forever, in the insurance contract. And they are vulnerable to 1970s-style inflation, because whatever annual increase you lock in when you buy the contract is all you're going to get.

I'd argue that both of these downsides look worse than they are. You effectively give up a lot of liquidity if you keep your investments in stocks and bonds and try to follow the 4% rule, because you can't use the money for a big-ticket expense and still allow it to compound to finance your 4% rule. And while you might think a stock-and-bond portfolio offers better protection against a big rise in inflation, that's a shaky argument.

The inflation of the 1970s proved a disaster for stocks and bonds. There's every reason to think a regular investment portfolio would suffer badly from a rerun of that scenario. Furthermore, annuity payout rates start so far above 4% or 4.5% that you have plenty of cushion before they turn into a comparatively worse deal.

Using annuities the right way

In any event, retirees are rarely advised to put all of their money into annuities.

"Higher payout rates make income annuities worth a fresh look, but only for money a client needs to turn into a paycheck, not money meant to grow," says Jeff Judge, a financial planner with Chesapeake Financial Planners in Forest Hill, Md. "I use annuities to cover essential bills, not to chase returns."

Juan Hernandez-Ariano, a financial planner with WealthCreate in Houston, Texas, says annuities like this can either be a great retirement tool or a very bad decision, depending on the individual's own circumstances. Current payout rates make them very attractive, he says, but adds: "I wouldn't use one for someone who'd have to put most of their savings in to make the numbers work, because there's no getting that money back for something like a hurricane deductible."

And Josh Norris, a financial planner with LeFleur Financial in Jackson, Miss., says the jump in payout rates is a bit of a red herring. "Whatever payout the annuity companies offer is based largely on what they can make on your money, and that's the return you forgo to buy their annuity."

He's right, but with one caveat. Insurance companies tend to buy bonds first and then use them to finance their new annuities, with the result that annuity payout rates tend to reflect the interest rates in the bond market from a few weeks ago. As a result, the juicy annuity rates on offer today reflect the historic interest rates seen on bonds in late September and early this month. Those bond rates have come down in the last few weeks, and if that continues, annuity rates can be expected to follow suit.

"Payout rates typically track to long-term yields with a lag," explains Keith Golembiewski, head of annuities research at the life-insurance trade association LIMRA. Those lags vary between insurance companies but typically are between two and four weeks, he adds.

What to watch for

Consumers should always look carefully at the terms and conditions of an annuity before assuming it's a good deal.

Hernandez-Ariano, a qualified insurance salesman, warns that those selling insurance are not held to the same high standards of fiduciary responsibility as financial planners. So always check what you are buying and who you are buying it from, and ask about their sales commissions.

A well-known place to shop for annuities is at immediateannuities.com, which is run by Hersh Stern, the company that published Annuity Shopper for decades.

Immediate, lifetime or guaranteed annuities should not be confused with various other products that are called annuities, such as indexed annuities, which are typically tax-advantaged savings and investment vehicles. The problems with so many of those include high fees and lock-in periods with hefty withdrawal penalties.

Beating inflation

If you really want inflation protection, nothing will beat inflation-protected Treasury bonds, known as TIPS. If I sound like a broken record on TIPS - and on guaranteed-income annuities, for that matter - there are good reasons for it. Both offer compelling tools for squaring the circle that many people face when they retire: squeezing out the maximum material standard of living for the rest of their life.

TIPS bonds are, by historic measures, somewhere between a good value and a ridiculous bargain, depending on whom you ask. Long-term TIPS yields are now between 2.5% and 3% a year plus the official inflation rate, whatever that turns out to be. For most of the last 20 years, TIPS were ridiculously overpriced, as part of the great zero-interest-rate bond bubble, and offered paltry yields.

Bonds are like seesaws: When the price rises, the yield or interest rate falls, and vice versa.

At several points during the last 20 years, TIPS sometimes offered negative real yields, meaning you were guaranteed to lose purchasing power over the life of the bond. I never understood why anyone would bet on a horse after it had lost a race. Various financial planners tried to explain it to me, and doubtless they had good reasons, but it seemed an unappealing option. And so it proved to be.

Today, on the other hand, those inflation-adjusted or "real" yields are at generational highs.

The main risk, as with any Treasury bonds, is that the insane U.S. budget deficits could lead to a budget crisis. On the other hand, anyone buying TIPS, even very long-term TIPS, has two advantages. First, a U.S. debt crisis would collapse the entire financial world, so even Congress wouldn't let it happen. (Also, everything else would fall, not just Treasury bonds.) Second, the most obvious, politically cowardly way out of our debt mess is through inflation - which would be OK for TIPS, if not for regular bonds.

But while TIPS might protect you against inflation, they won't protect you against longevity. That's why people are often advised to buy annuities.

-Brett Arends
